fields.title: The Gospel of Matthew
fields.subtitle: Kata Maththaion, “According to Matthew”
fields.description: The first book of the New Testament, which opens with a family line from Abraham through David to “Jesus, who is called Christ”, and shows again and again that in him the promises of Israel’s Scriptures were fulfilled. The wise men and their star; the Sermon on the Mount, with the beatitudes and the Lord’s Prayer; parables of the kingdom of heaven, from the mustard seed to the pearl of great price; Peter’s confession and the promise of the church; the sheep and the goats; the cross, the guarded tomb, and the risen Lord sending his disciples to make disciples of all the nations, with the promise “I myself am with you every day, until the close of the age.” In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Gospel of Matthew?
qa.answer: The first of the four Gospels, the accounts of the life, death and resurrection of Jesus in the New Testament, and for most of the church’s history the most read of them. It presents Jesus as the son of David and the son of Abraham, Israel’s Messiah, in whom the Scriptures are fulfilled, and gathers his teaching into five long speeches, beginning with the Sermon on the Mount (chapters 5–7). It ends with the risen Jesus sending his disciples to all the nations (28:18–20).

qa.question: Who wrote the Gospel of Matthew, and when?
qa.answer: The Gospel does not name its author. From the second century the church gave it to Matthew, the tax collector who became one of the Twelve (9:9). Papias, early in the second century, said that Matthew wrote the oracles in the Hebrew language. Most scholars today think the author drew on Mark’s Gospel and date the book to the decades after AD 70; others hold that Matthew wrote first, or date it in the 60s.

qa.question: Why does Matthew say “kingdom of heaven” instead of “kingdom of God”?
qa.answer: Devout Jews often said “heaven” rather than speak the name of God too freely, and Matthew, writing as a Jew for readers who knew the Scriptures, follows their custom. The kingdom of heaven is not a different kingdom from the kingdom of God in Mark and Luke, and it does not mean only a place people go when they die. It is God’s own rule, which Jesus says “has come near” (4:17).

qa.question: What are the five speeches in Matthew?
qa.answer: Matthew gathers Jesus’s teaching into five long speeches, each ending with almost the same words, “When Jesus had finished”: the Sermon on the Mount (5–7), the sending of the Twelve (10), the parables of the kingdom (13), life together in the community of disciples (18), and the end of the age (24–25). Between them come stories of what Jesus did. Many readers have heard an echo of the five books of Moses.

qa.question: What does Matthew 16:18 mean by “on this rock I will build my church”?
qa.answer: Jesus plays on Peter’s name, which means rock, after Peter confesses him as the Christ, the Son of the living God. Christians have long differed on what the rock is: Peter himself, as the first of the apostles; the faith he has just confessed; or Christ, the only foundation. Matthew is the only Gospel in which Jesus speaks of the church, here and in 18:17.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
The record of the family line of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham.

— Matthew 1:1

Open the New Testament and the first thing you meet is a list of names. It is not a false start. Matthew’s first words, in Greek, are the words that open the account of heaven and earth and the list of Adam’s descendants in the Greek Old Testament (Genesis 2:4; 5:1). Before he has told us a single thing Jesus did, he has told us that this story is the next chapter of the old one, and its fulfilment.

The list says so too. It runs from Abraham, to whom God promised that all nations would be blessed, through David, to whom God promised a king whose kingdom would never end, to “Jesus, who is called Christ”. Matthew arranges it in three sets of fourteen generations: from Abraham to David, from David to the exile in Babylon, and from the exile to the Messiah. Israel’s whole history, its rise, its fall and its long waiting, has been leading to this child.

That is the key to the whole book. Matthew is the Gospel of the promises kept. It was written by a Jew, steeped in the Scriptures of Israel, for readers who needed to see that Jesus was not a break with everything God had said before but the point of it all. And it ends, as the old story never quite could, with the nations of the world drawn in.

The first Gospel

Matthew has stood first among the four Gospels for as long as there have been four, and for most of the church’s history it was the most read, the most quoted and the most preached of them. It is the Gospel of the Sermon on the Mount and the Lord’s Prayer as most Christians pray it, of the wise men and their star, of Peter walking on the water and the parable of the sheep and the goats. It reads like a book made to be taught.

Like the other Gospels, it does not name its author. From the second century the church gave it to Matthew, one of the Twelve, the tax collector whose calling it tells in a single verse:

Moving on from there, Jesus noticed a man called Matthew at his seat in the tax office. Jesus said to him, “Follow me.” And Matthew rose and followed him.

— Matthew 9:9

Mark and Luke tell the same story of a tax collector named Levi; only this Gospel calls him Matthew. Papias, a bishop in Asia Minor early in the second century, is quoted by the historian Eusebius as saying that “Matthew wrote the oracles in the Hebrew language, and every one interpreted them as he was able”, and Irenaeus, around 180, says that Matthew issued a written Gospel among the Hebrews in their own dialect. What Papias meant is still debated, since the Gospel we have reads like a book composed in Greek.

Most scholars today think Matthew drew on Mark’s Gospel, which he follows closely and nearly all of which he contains, along with a collection of Jesus’s sayings that he shares with Luke. Others hold, as Augustine did, that Matthew came first. Many date the book to the decades after the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70; others put it earlier, in the 60s. On any view its author knew the Jewish world from the inside, and the questions it was asking about Jesus.

Five great sermons

Matthew gathers Jesus’s teaching into five long speeches, each ending with almost the same words: “When Jesus finished these words”, “When Jesus had finished giving these instructions”, “When Jesus had finished telling these parables”, and so on. Between them come stories of what Jesus did. The book moves back and forth, deed and word, like a weaver’s shuttle:

  • The Sermon on the Mount (5–7): the life of the kingdom, from the beatitudes to the house built on rock.
  • The sending of the Twelve (10): how the disciples are to go out, and what they will suffer.
  • The parables of the kingdom (13): the sower, the weeds, the mustard seed, the treasure, the pearl and the net.
  • Life together (18): little ones, lost sheep, a brother who sins, and forgiveness without limit.
  • The end of the age (24–25): the fall of the temple, the coming of the Son of Man, and three parables of readiness.

Many readers have heard in the five an echo of the five books of Moses, and seen Jesus as a new Moses who teaches from a mountain. Matthew does not say so, and the echo should not be pressed. But the parallel with Moses is there from the start: a wicked king who kills the baby boys, a child saved by flight, a return from Egypt, forty days in the wilderness, and then a mountain and a teaching. The difference is that Moses received the law from God. Jesus speaks it in his own name: “But I tell you.”

Promises kept

About ten times Matthew stops the story to say that something happened “so that the word the Lord had spoken through the prophet would be fulfilled”, and quotes the verse. The virgin conceives; the child is born in Bethlehem; he is called out of Egypt; he settles in Galilee, “where the Gentiles live”; he heals the sick, rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, and is sold for thirty silver coins. No other Gospel quotes the Old Testament so often or so deliberately.

These quotations can puzzle modern readers, because the verses often meant something in their first setting that does not look like a prediction. Hosea’s “Out of Egypt I called my son” is about Israel leaving Egypt in the exodus. But that is exactly Matthew’s point. Jesus does not only fulfil a handful of forecasts; he lives Israel’s story over again, and gets it right. Israel was God’s son, called out of Egypt, tested in the wilderness and found wanting. Jesus is God’s Son, called out of Egypt, tested in the wilderness for forty days, and faithful. At his baptism he tells John that this is the fitting way “to fulfill all righteousness”, and he says the same of the whole of Scripture:

Do not suppose that I have come to do away with the law or the prophets. I have not come to do away with them but to fulfill them.

— Matthew 5:17

The kingdom of heaven

John the Baptist’s message and Jesus’s are the same, word for word: “Repent, because the kingdom of heaven has come near.” Where Mark and Luke say “the kingdom of God”, Matthew almost always says “the kingdom of heaven”, a phrase found nowhere else in the New Testament. It is not a different kingdom, and it does not mean a place we go when we die. Devout Jews often spoke of “heaven” to avoid saying the name of God too freely, and Matthew follows their custom. The kingdom of heaven is God’s own rule, breaking into the world in the person of Jesus.

The parables of chapter 13 explain what kind of kingdom it is. It starts small, like a mustard seed. It grows unseen, like yeast in the dough. For now it grows alongside the weeds, and the sorting is left to the harvest. And it is worth everything: a man finds treasure buried in a field and, “full of joy”, sells all he owns to buy that field; a trader finds a single pearl of very high price and does the same. The chapter ends with a picture that may be Matthew’s own portrait of himself, a scribe trained for the kingdom, who brings out of his storeroom “both new things and old”.

The Sermon on the Mount

The first of the five speeches is the most famous sermon ever preached. It opens with a list of the happy that turns the world’s list upside down:

“Blessed are those who are poor in spirit: the kingdom of heaven is theirs. Blessed are those who mourn: they will be comforted. Blessed are the gentle: they will inherit the earth.

— Matthew 5:3–5

Then it goes deeper than any law court can reach. Six times Jesus quotes what had been said (“You have heard…”) and goes beyond it: not only murder but anger, not only adultery but the look that wants, not only fair revenge but turning the other cheek, not only love for a neighbour but love for an enemy. He calls for a righteousness that “goes far beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees”, and he ends that part of the sermon with words that have humbled every reader since: “You, then, are to be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.”

Christians have read the sermon in many ways: as a law for every disciple, as a counsel of perfection for the few, as a mirror that shows us our need of grace, as the ethic of the kingdom still to come. Most have found some truth in more than one of these. But the sermon itself does not let anyone admire it from a distance. Its centre is the Lord’s Prayer, a prayer to a Father who already knows what his children need. Its rule of life is short enough to memorise: “treat others the way you would want them to treat you.” And it ends not with an idea but with two houses, one on rock and one on sand, and a storm that comes to both. The difference is whether we listen to Jesus’s words and act on them.

God with us

Near the beginning of the book an angel tells Joseph to name the child Jesus, “because he is the one who will save his people from their sins.” Then Matthew adds a second name, from Isaiah:

“See, the virgin will become pregnant and have a son, and people will call him Immanuel.” The name means “God is with us.”

— Matthew 1:23

Matthew returns to that name at the middle of his Gospel and at the end. In chapter 18 Jesus promises that wherever two or three come together in his name, “I am there among them.” And the last words of the book are a promise: “I myself am with you every day, until the close of the age.” The Gospel is framed by God’s presence. Jesus is not only the teacher of Israel and the fulfilment of its Scriptures. He is the one in whom God has come to be with his people, and he does not leave.

For Israel, and for the nations

Matthew is the most Jewish of the Gospels. It assumes its readers know about the Sabbath, the temple tax and the washing of hands. Jesus is the son of David, the king of the Jews, the Messiah of Israel. When he first sends out the Twelve he tells them to stay off the roads that lead to the Gentiles and go “to the lost sheep, the people of Israel”, and he says the same of himself.

And yet it is also the Gospel that opens most widely to the world. Four women appear in the family line, all of them, it seems, outsiders in one way or another: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and “the wife of Uriah”. The first people to worship the infant king are magi from the east, Gentile stargazers, while Jerusalem’s king tries to kill him. A Roman centurion shows faith such as Jesus has found nowhere in Israel, and Jesus says that many will come from east and west to eat with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. A Canaanite woman, whom the disciples want sent away, will not be put off, and goes home with her daughter healed and these words ringing in her ears: “Woman, your faith is great.” At the cross it is a centurion and his soldiers who say, “This man truly was God’s Son!”

So when the risen Jesus sends the eleven out to “all the nations”, he is not changing his mind. He is completing what was promised to Abraham at the head of the family list: that through his offspring all the peoples of the earth would be blessed.

Peter and the church

Matthew is the only Gospel in which Jesus speaks of the church, and he does so twice. The first time is at Caesarea Philippi, at the turning point of the book. Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is, and then who they say he is:

Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

— Matthew 16:16

Jesus answers that no human being showed Peter this, but the Father, and then plays on his name, which means rock: “you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church.” Christians have long differed over what the rock is: Peter himself, as the first of the apostles; the faith he has just confessed; or Christ, the only foundation. The second time is in chapter 18, where the church is a small and very practical thing, a gathering of brothers and sisters who must learn to deal honestly with sin among them and forgive one another, not seven times but seventy-seven.

Matthew does not flatter the church’s first leader. A few verses after his great confession Peter tries to talk Jesus out of the cross and is called Satan. He walks on the water and sinks. He swears he will never desert Jesus and denies him three times before a rooster crows. The rock on which the church is built is a man who needs to be caught by the hand.

The king on the cross

The last chapters of Matthew follow Mark closely, but add details of their own: Judas’s remorse and death, the dream of Pilate’s wife, Pilate washing his hands, the earthquake at Jesus’s death and the guard at the tomb. Over the cross hangs the charge, “This is Jesus, the King of the Jews”, and Matthew wants his readers to see that it is true. The king of Israel is enthroned between two criminals.

One verse in these chapters needs a careful word. When Pilate washes his hands of Jesus’s death, the crowd gathered before him shouts, “Let the guilt for his death fall on us and on our children!” For centuries that cry was used to blame the Jewish people as a whole for the crucifixion and to justify hatred and violence against them. The text does not support that use. Matthew reports what a crowd, stirred up by its leaders, shouted on one morning. Jesus, his disciples and the women at the cross were all Jews; and in this Gospel Jesus’s blood is “poured out for many to bring forgiveness of sins”.

The resurrection in Matthew comes with an earthquake and an angel like lightning, who rolls back the stone and sits on it. The guards become like dead men; the women run off with fear and great joy, and meet Jesus himself on the road. And the book ends on a mountain in Galilee, where the eleven worship him, “but some had doubts”. It is an honest touch, and a hopeful one: Jesus sends them out anyway.

How to read Matthew

Read it first for its shape. The birth and childhood (1–2) and the beginning of Jesus’s work (3–4) lead into the alternation of speeches and stories (5–25), and then into the passion and resurrection (26–28). Notice the five speeches and the words that close each one. Notice the turning point at 16:21, where Jesus begins to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer.

Then read it slowly, with the Old Testament open. When Matthew says something was fulfilled, look up the verse and ask what it meant in its first setting, and why he thought it came true in Jesus. Notice how often Jesus says “Truly I tell you”, and how often he says “something greater” is here: greater than the temple, greater than Jonah, greater than Solomon.

And read the Sermon on the Mount as Jesus meant it, not only as teaching to admire but as words to build a life on.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Matthew are worth knowing about before you begin.

“The kingdom of heaven.” The translation keeps Matthew’s own phrase rather than changing it to “the kingdom of God”, so that readers can follow it through the book.

The beatitudes. Each is printed in two halves, the blessing and the promise, joined by a colon: “Blessed are the merciful: mercy will be shown to them.” Where older Bibles say “the meek”, this one says “the gentle”, since “meek” can now suggest weakness.

The Lord’s Prayer. It asks God not to lead us “into testing” and to “rescue us from the evil one”. The familiar closing words of praise, “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory”, are not in the earliest manuscripts; the church added them in its worship, and this translation ends the prayer where Matthew did.

Verses not found in the oldest manuscripts. Matthew 17:21, 18:11 and 23:14, which older Bibles print, are missing from the earliest copies and were probably added from Mark and Luke. They are not in the text, and the verse numbers are skipped. In 27:16–17 the prisoner whom Pilate offers the crowd is called by his full name, Jesus Barabbas, as some early manuscripts have it: Pilate asks whether they want “Jesus Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ”.

“Christ.” The Open Word Bible lets a reader choose whether Christos reads “Christ” or “the Messiah”. This edition prints “Christ”, but in Matthew above all it is worth remembering that the word means Israel’s anointed King, the son of David.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Greek beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Matthew 1
fields.body_html:
The ancestors of Jesus

The record of the family line of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham. Abraham was the father of Isaac, Isaac of Jacob, and Jacob of Judah and his brothers. Judah was the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar. Perez was the father of Hezron, and Hezron of Ram. Ram was the father of Amminadab, Amminadab of Nahshon, and Nahshon of Salmon. Salmon was the father of Boaz by Rahab. Boaz was the father of Obed by Ruth. Obed was the father of Jesse, and Jesse was the father of David the king. David was the father of Solomon by the wife of Uriah. Solomon was the father of Rehoboam, Rehoboam of Abijah, and Abijah of Asa. Asa was the father of Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat of Joram, and Joram of Uzziah. Uzziah was the father of Jotham, Jotham of Ahaz, and Ahaz of Hezekiah. Hezekiah was the father of Manasseh, Manasseh of Amon, and Amon of Josiah. Josiah was the father of Jechoniah and his brothers at the time of the deportation to Babylon.

After the deportation to Babylon, Jechoniah was the father of Shealtiel, and Shealtiel of Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel was the father of Abiud, Abiud of Eliakim, and Eliakim of Azor. Azor was the father of Zadok, Zadok of Achim, and Achim of Eliud. Eliud was the father of Eleazar, Eleazar of Matthan, and Matthan of Jacob. Jacob was the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, and of Mary was born Jesus, who is called Christ.

So there were fourteen generations in all from Abraham to David, fourteen from David to the deportation to Babylon, and fourteen from the deportation to Babylon to Christ.

The birth of Jesus

Now this is how Jesus Christ came to be born. His mother Mary was pledged to be married to Joseph, but before they began to live together it became clear that she was expecting a child through the Holy Spirit. Joseph her husband was a righteous man and did not want to disgrace her in public, so he decided to divorce her privately. While he was turning this over in his mind, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream. “Joseph, son of David,” he said, “do not be afraid to take Mary into your home as your wife. The child she has conceived is from the Holy Spirit. She will give birth to a son, and you are to name him Jesus, because he is the one who will save his people from their sins.” All this happened so that the word the Lord had spoken through the prophet would be fulfilled: “See, the virgin will become pregnant and have a son, and people will call him Immanuel.” The name means “God is with us.” Joseph got up from his sleep and did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him. He took his wife into his home. But he did not have sexual relations with her until she had given birth to a son, and he named him Jesus.
fields.summary: The genealogy of Jesus runs from Abraham through David to Joseph, the husband of Mary. An angel tells Joseph in a dream that the child conceived in Mary is from the Holy Spirit, and Joseph names the child Jesus.

fields.title: Matthew 2
fields.body_html:
The magi visit the child

When Jesus had been born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the days of King Herod, magi from the east arrived in Jerusalem with a question: “Where is the newborn king of the Jews? We saw his star when it rose, and we have come to worship him.” When King Herod heard this, he was shaken, and so was all Jerusalem. He called together all the chief priests and the scribes of the people and asked them where the Christ was to be born. “In Bethlehem in Judea,” they told him, “because this is what the prophet wrote: ‘And you, Bethlehem, in the land of Judah, are far from the least among the leading towns of Judah, for from you will come a leader who will be the shepherd of my people Israel.’”

Herod then summoned the magi in private and questioned them to learn the exact time the star had appeared. He sent them on to Bethlehem with these words: “Go and find out all you can about the child. When you have found him, send word back to me, so that I may come and worship him as well.” They listened to the king and set out. And there was the star they had seen at its rising, going ahead of them, until it came and stood over the place where the child was. The sight of the star filled them with a very great joy. Entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother. They fell to the ground and worshiped him, and they opened their chests of treasure and offered him gifts: gold, frankincense and myrrh. And since they had been warned in a dream not to go back to Herod, they went home to their own country by a different road.

The escape to Egypt

When the magi had gone, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and told him, “Get up and flee to Egypt with the child and his mother. Remain there until I give you word, for Herod means to hunt for the child and destroy him.” Joseph got up, took the child and his mother while it was still night, and left for Egypt. He stayed there until Herod died, so that the word the Lord had spoken through the prophet would be fulfilled: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”

Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem

When Herod saw that the magi had made a fool of him, he was furious. He sent soldiers and killed all the boys in Bethlehem and the area around it who were two years old or younger, in keeping with the time he had found out from the magi. Then the word spoken through the prophet Jeremiah was fulfilled: “A sound was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud wailing: Rachel crying for her children and refusing all comfort, because they are gone.”

The return to Nazareth

After Herod died, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt and said, “Get up, take the child and his mother, and go back to the land of Israel, because those who wanted the child dead have died.” Joseph got up, took the child and his mother, and went into the land of Israel. But when he heard that Archelaus had succeeded his father Herod as ruler of Judea, he was afraid to go there. Warned in a dream, he went instead to the region of Galilee and made his home in a town called Nazareth. This was so that what the prophets had said would be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.
fields.summary: Magi from the east follow a star to Bethlehem and worship the child. Warned in a dream, Joseph takes the family to Egypt while Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem, and after Herod dies they settle in Nazareth.

fields.title: Matthew 3
fields.body_html:
John the Baptist prepares the way

In those days John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness of Judea with a message. “Repent,” he proclaimed, “because the kingdom of heaven has come near.” John is the one the prophet Isaiah spoke of when he said, “A voice is calling out in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord, straighten the roads he will travel.’” John himself dressed in clothing woven from camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey. Crowds kept coming out to him from Jerusalem, from all over Judea, and from all the country along the Jordan. They confessed their sins, and he baptized them in the Jordan River.

But when John saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming for baptism, he said to them, “You family of snakes! Who warned you to run from the coming wrath? So produce fruit that shows your repentance is real. Do not imagine you can comfort yourselves by saying, ‘Abraham is our father.’ I tell you, God is able to make children for Abraham out of these stones. The ax is already set against the root of the trees. Any tree that fails to bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.

I baptize you with water for repentance. But one who comes after me is mightier than I am, and I am not fit even to carry his sandals. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire. He has his winnowing fork in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor. He will gather his wheat into the barn, but he will burn up the chaff with a fire that cannot be put out.”

The baptism of Jesus

Then Jesus arrived from Galilee and came to John at the Jordan, to be baptized by him. John tried to stop him. “I am the one who needs to be baptized by you,” he said, “and yet you come to me?” But Jesus answered, “Allow it for now. This is the fitting way for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then John let him be baptized. Jesus was baptized, and he came straight up out of the water. Suddenly the heavens opened, and he saw the Spirit of God coming down like a dove and settling on him. And a voice spoke from heaven: “This is my dearly loved Son, and I delight in him.”
fields.summary: John the Baptist preaches repentance in the wilderness of Judea and baptizes in the Jordan. When Jesus is baptized, the Spirit of God comes down like a dove and a voice from heaven names Jesus as God’s beloved Son.

fields.title: Matthew 4
fields.body_html:
The testing of Jesus

Then the Spirit led Jesus up into the wilderness, where the devil would tempt him. He fasted forty days and forty nights, and at the end of it he was famished. Then the tempter approached him. “If you are the Son of God,” he said, “command these stones to become loaves of bread.” But Jesus answered, “Scripture says, ‘No one lives on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.’”

Then the devil brought him to the holy city and set him on the high corner of the temple. “If you are the Son of God,” he told him, “jump down. For Scripture says, ‘He will put his angels in charge of you,’ and, ‘They will catch you in their hands, so that you will not strike your foot against a stone.’” Jesus answered him, “Scripture says something else as well: ‘You must not test the Lord your God.’”

Then the devil led him up a very high mountain and showed him every kingdom of the world in all its glory. “I will give you all of this,” he told him, “if you kneel down and worship me.” “Get away, Satan!” Jesus said to him. “For Scripture says, ‘You must worship the Lord your God and serve no one but him.’” Then the devil left him, and angels came and took care of him.

Jesus begins in Galilee

News reached Jesus that John had been arrested, and he went back to Galilee. He left Nazareth and went to live in Capernaum, a town by the sea in the region of Zebulun and Naphtali. This was so that the word spoken through the prophet Isaiah would be fulfilled: “Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, along the road by the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee where the Gentiles live: the people who sat in darkness saw a great light, and for those who sat in the land of death’s shadow, light rose like the dawn.”

From then on Jesus began to proclaim, “Repent, because the kingdom of heaven has come near.”

The first disciples

As Jesus walked along the shore of the Sea of Galilee, he noticed two brothers, Simon, also called Peter, and Andrew his brother, throwing a net into the water. They fished for a living. “Come, follow me,” he said to them, “and I will make you fishers of people.” They left their nets at once and followed him.

A little farther on he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in their boat with Zebedee their father, repairing their nets. He called them. They left the boat and their father without delay and followed him.

Teaching and healing in Galilee

Jesus went from place to place all over Galilee. He taught in their synagogues, announced the gospel of the kingdom, and healed every disease and every illness among the people. News about him spread through all Syria, and people brought to him everyone who was ill: those suffering from all kinds of diseases and pain, people controlled by demons, people who had seizures, and people who could not move. And he healed them. Great crowds followed him from Galilee, the Decapolis, Jerusalem, Judea, and the region beyond the Jordan.
fields.summary: The devil tests Jesus in the wilderness, and Jesus answers each time from Scripture. In Galilee Jesus begins to proclaim the kingdom of heaven, calls four fishermen, and teaches and heals throughout the region.

fields.title: Matthew 5
fields.body_html:
The Sermon on the Mount

Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up onto the mountain. He sat down, and his disciples came to him. And he began to teach them: “Blessed are those who are poor in spirit: the kingdom of heaven is theirs. Blessed are those who mourn: they will be comforted. Blessed are the gentle: they will inherit the earth. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness: they will be satisfied. Blessed are the merciful: mercy will be shown to them. Blessed are the pure in heart: they will see God. Blessed are those who make peace: they will be called children of God. Blessed are those who suffer persecution for the sake of righteousness: the kingdom of heaven is theirs. You are blessed when people abuse you and persecute you and spread all sorts of evil lies about you for my sake. Rejoice and celebrate, because a great reward is waiting for you in heaven. That is how they persecuted the prophets who came before you.

Salt and light

You are the salt for the earth. But if salt goes flat, what can give it back its saltiness? It is good for nothing anymore but to be thrown out and walked on.

You are the light of the world. A town built on a hilltop cannot be hidden. No one lights a lamp and hides it under a basket; it goes on a lampstand, where it shines for everyone in the house. In the same way, your light must shine where people can see it, so that they will see your good deeds and give glory to your Father in heaven.

Jesus and the law

Do not suppose that I have come to do away with the law or the prophets. I have not come to do away with them but to fulfill them. Truly I tell you, as long as heaven and earth last, not one tiny letter or even part of a letter will vanish from the law until all of it comes about. So anyone who loosens even the smallest of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But anyone who obeys them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. For I tell you, unless your righteousness goes far beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.

Anger

You have heard what our ancestors were told: ‘Do not commit murder. Whoever commits murder must answer for it in court.’ But I tell you that anyone who is angry with a brother or sister will have to answer for it in court. Anyone who says to a brother or sister, ‘You empty-head,’ will answer to the high council. And anyone who says, ‘You fool,’ will be in danger of the fire of hell. So if you are bringing your offering to the altar and there you remember that a brother or sister has something against you, leave your offering there in front of the altar. Go and make peace with them first, and then come back and offer your gift. If someone is taking you to court, settle with them quickly while you are still on the way there. Otherwise your accuser may hand you over to the judge, the judge may hand you over to the guard, and you may be thrown into prison. Truly I tell you, you will not get out until you have paid the last penny.

Adultery

You have heard the commandment, ‘Do not commit adultery.’ But I tell you, a man who looks at a woman with the aim of wanting her for himself has already committed adultery with her in his heart. If your right eye leads you into sin, pull it out and get rid of it. You are better off losing one part of your body than having all of you thrown into hell. And if your right hand leads you into sin, cut it off and get rid of it. You are better off losing one part of your body than having all of you go into hell.

Divorce

It was also said, ‘A man who sends his wife away must give her a written notice of divorce.’ But I tell you that a man who divorces his wife for any reason other than sexual unfaithfulness causes her to commit adultery, and anyone who marries a woman who has been divorced commits adultery.

Oaths

You have also heard what our ancestors were told: ‘Do not swear falsely. Do what you have promised the Lord with an oath.’ But I tell you, do not take an oath at all, not by heaven, because it is God’s throne, or by the earth, because it is his footstool, or by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King. Do not swear by your own head either, since you cannot turn a single hair white or black. Let your yes be yes and your no be no. Whatever you add to that comes from the evil one.

Do not take revenge

You have heard the saying, ‘Eye for eye, tooth for tooth.’ But I tell you, do not fight back against an evil person. If anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn the other cheek to them as well. If someone wants to take you to court and take your shirt, let them have your coat as well. If someone forces you to carry a load one mile, go two miles with them. Give to anyone who asks you, and do not turn your back on someone who wants to borrow from you.

Love your enemies

You have heard the saying, ‘Love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I tell you: love your enemies, and pray for the people who persecute you, so that you will be children of your Father in heaven. He makes his sun rise on evil people and good people alike, and he sends rain on those who do right and those who do wrong. If you love the people who love you, what reward is there in that? Even tax collectors do that, do they not? And if you greet only your own brothers and sisters, what are you doing that is out of the ordinary? Even the Gentiles do that, do they not? You, then, are to be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
fields.summary: On a mountain Jesus begins the Sermon on the Mount with the blessings, calls the disciples salt and light, and says the law is not abolished but fulfilled. Jesus goes deeper than the commandments on anger, adultery, divorce, oaths and revenge, and commands love for enemies.

fields.title: Matthew 6
fields.body_html:
Not for show

Take care not to put your righteousness on show for others to see. If you do, your Father in heaven has no reward for you.

So when you give to the poor, do not announce it with trumpets, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and on the streets to win praise from others. Truly I tell you, they have already been paid in full. But when you give, keep it so quiet that your left hand does not know what your right hand is doing. Your gift will be hidden, and your Father, who sees what is hidden, will repay you.

Prayer

And when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites. They love to stand and pray in the synagogues and at the street corners where others can see them. Truly I tell you, they have been paid in full. But when you pray, go into an inner room, shut the door, and pray to your Father who is there in secret. Your Father sees what is hidden, and he will repay you.

When you pray, do not keep piling up empty words as the pagans do. They think they will be heard because they say so much. So do not imitate them. Your Father already knows what you need before you ask him.

The Lord’s Prayer

So this is how you should pray: ‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. May your kingdom come. May your will be done on earth, as it is done in heaven. Give us today the bread we need. Forgive us what we owe you, as we too have forgiven those who owe us. And do not lead us into testing, but rescue us from the evil one.’ For if you forgive others when they wrong you, your Father in heaven will forgive you as well. But if you refuse to forgive others, your Father will not forgive your wrongs either.

Fasting

When you fast, do not put on a sad face as the hypocrites do. They make their faces look gloomy so that others will see they are fasting. Truly I tell you, they have been paid in full. But when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face, so that no one but your Father, who is there in secret, will know that you are fasting. Your Father sees what is hidden, and he will repay you.

Treasure in heaven

Do not pile up treasures for yourselves on earth, where moths and rust ruin them and thieves dig through walls and steal them. Instead, pile up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where no moth or rust can ruin them and no thief can dig through and steal. Your heart will always be where your treasure is.

The eye is the lamp of the body. So if your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light. But if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. So if the light inside you is really darkness, how deep that darkness is!

No one can serve two masters. Either they will hate one and love the other, or they will be loyal to one and look down on the other. You cannot serve both God and money.

Do not worry

That is why I tell you not to worry about your life, about what you will eat, or about your body, about what you will wear. Is life not more than food, and the body more than clothes? Look at the birds in the sky. They do not plant or harvest or store food in barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth far more than they are? Can any of you add a single hour to your life by worrying? And why do you worry about clothes? Think about how the wildflowers grow. They neither toil nor spin thread. But I tell you, Solomon in all his glory was never dressed as beautifully as one of them. If that is how God clothes the wild grass, which is here today and thrown into the oven tomorrow, will he not clothe you much more, you who have so little faith? So do not worry and say, ‘What will we eat?’ or, ‘What will we drink?’ or, ‘What will we wear?’ The pagans chase after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. Above all, seek the kingdom and his righteousness, and you will be given all these things as well. So do not be troubled about tomorrow; tomorrow can take care of its own worries. Today’s trouble is enough for today.
fields.summary: Jesus warns against giving, praying and fasting for show and teaches the Lord’s Prayer. Treasure in heaven matters more than wealth, and those who seek God’s kingdom first need not worry about tomorrow.

fields.title: Matthew 7
fields.body_html:
Judging others

Stop passing judgment on others, so that you will not be judged. The way you judge others is the way you will be judged, and the measure you use for them will be used for you. Why do you stare at the splinter in the eye of a brother or sister, and never notice the beam of wood in your own? How can you say to a brother or sister, ‘Let me take that splinter out of your eye,’ when all the time there is a beam in your own? You hypocrite! First take the beam out of your own eye. Then you will see clearly enough to take the splinter out of the eye of a brother or sister.

Do not give holy things to dogs, and do not throw your pearls to pigs. They may trample them underfoot and then turn on you and tear you apart.

Ask, seek, knock

Keep asking, and you will receive. Keep seeking, and you will find. Keep knocking, and the door will be opened for you. For everyone who asks receives, whoever seeks finds, and the door is opened to whoever knocks. Would any of you give your child a stone when they asked for bread? Or give them a snake when they asked for a fish? So if you, sinful as you are, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask him!

So in everything, treat others the way you would want them to treat you, for this is what the law and the prophets are about.

The narrow gate

Go in through the narrow gate. The gate that leads to destruction is wide and the road to it is easy, and many go in that way. But the gate that leads to life is narrow and the road is hard, and only a few find it.

Known by their fruit

Watch out for false prophets. They come to you looking like sheep, but underneath they are hungry wolves. You will know them by what their lives produce. Do people pick grapes from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? In the same way, every healthy tree bears good fruit, and a diseased tree bears bad fruit. A healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit, and a diseased tree cannot bear good fruit. Any tree that fails to bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. So you will know them by what their lives produce.

I never knew you

Not everyone who calls me ‘Lord, Lord’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only those who do what my Father in heaven wants. On that day many will say to me, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, drive out demons in your name, and do many miracles in your name?’ And then I will say to them openly, ‘I never knew you. Go away from me, you who break God’s law.’

Two builders

So anyone who listens to what I have said here and acts on it will be like a sensible person who built a house on solid rock. The rain poured down, the floods rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house. But it did not fall, because its foundation was on rock. And anyone who listens to what I have said here and does not act on it will be like a foolish person who built a house on sand. The rain poured down, the floods rose, and the winds blew and battered that house, and it fell. And what a fall it was!”

Teaching with authority

When Jesus finished these words, the crowds were amazed at his teaching. He taught them like someone with authority of his own, not like their scribes.
fields.summary: Jesus warns against judging others, urges asking, seeking and knocking, and points to the narrow gate and to prophets known by their fruit. The sermon ends with two builders, one on rock and one on sand, and the crowds are amazed at teaching with authority.

fields.title: Matthew 8
fields.body_html:
Jesus heals a man with leprosy

Great crowds followed Jesus as he came down from the mountain. Just then a man with leprosy came up and bowed down before him. “Lord,” he said, “if you want to, you can make me clean.” Jesus reached out his hand and touched him. “I do want to,” he said. “Be clean!” At once his leprosy was gone. Then Jesus said to him, “Be sure you do not tell anyone. Instead, go and let the priest examine you, and offer the gift Moses commanded, as evidence for them.”

The centurion’s faith

When Jesus went into Capernaum, a centurion came to him and pleaded with him. “Lord,” he said, “my servant is lying at home, paralyzed and in terrible pain.” Jesus said to him, “I will come and heal him.” The centurion replied, “Lord, I am not good enough for you to come into my house. Only give the command, and my servant will be well. I myself am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. I tell one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and another, ‘Come,’ and he comes. I tell my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” Jesus was amazed when he heard this. He said to those who were following him, “Truly I tell you, nowhere in Israel have I found faith as great as this. I tell you, many will come from the east and the west and will sit down to eat with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. But those who were born heirs of the kingdom will be thrown out into the darkness outside, where people will weep and grind their teeth.” Then Jesus said to the centurion, “Go. It will happen for you just as you believed.” And the servant was healed in that same hour.

Healing at Peter’s house

Jesus went into Peter’s house and saw Peter’s mother-in-law lying in bed with a fever. He touched her hand, and the fever left her. She got up and began to wait on him.

That evening people brought him many who were controlled by demons. He drove out the spirits with a word and healed everyone who was sick. This was so that the word spoken through the prophet Isaiah would be fulfilled: “He took our weaknesses and carried our diseases.”

The cost of following Jesus

When Jesus saw the crowds gathering around him, he gave orders to cross to the other side of the lake. A scribe came up and said to him, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” Jesus told him, “Foxes have their holes and the birds in the sky their nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to rest his head.” Another of the disciples said to him, “Lord, allow me first to go away and bury my father.” But Jesus told him, “Follow me. Leave the dead to bury their own dead.”

Jesus calms the storm

Then Jesus stepped into the boat, and his disciples followed him. Without warning a great storm broke over the lake, and waves were sweeping over the boat. But he was asleep. They came and woke him. “Lord, save us!” they cried. “We are about to die!” He said to them, “Why are you so frightened, you who have so little faith?” Then he got up and spoke sharply to the winds and the waves, and everything became completely calm. They were amazed. “What kind of person is this?” they said. “Even the winds and the sea obey him!” When Jesus arrived on the other side, in the region of the Gadarenes, two men controlled by demons came out of the tombs to meet him. They were so dangerous that nobody dared to use that road. They screamed, “Son of God, what business do you have with us? Have you come here to torment us before the appointed time?” Some distance away a large herd of pigs was feeding. The demons kept begging him, “If you drive us out, send us into the herd of pigs.” “Go!” he told them. The demons came out and entered the pigs, and at once the whole herd stampeded down the slope into the lake and drowned. The men looking after the pigs ran off into the town and reported everything, including what had happened to the men with demons. At that the whole town came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him to go away from their district.
fields.summary: Jesus heals a man with leprosy, a centurion’s servant and Peter’s mother-in-law, and speaks of the cost of following. Jesus calms a storm on the lake and frees two men from demons, which go into a herd of pigs.

fields.title: Matthew 9
fields.body_html:
Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man

So Jesus got back into the boat, crossed the lake, and came to the town where he lived.

Some people brought him a paralyzed man lying on a stretcher. Jesus saw their faith and said to the man, “Be encouraged, my son. Your sins are forgiven.” At this some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is insulting God!” Jesus knew what they were thinking and said, “Why do you think such evil things in your hearts? Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’? But I want you to know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.” Then he said to the paralyzed man, “Get up, pick up your stretcher, and go home.” And the man got up and went home. When the crowds saw this, they were filled with awe, and they glorified God for giving such authority to human beings.

The call of Matthew

Moving on from there, Jesus noticed a man called Matthew at his seat in the tax office. Jesus said to him, “Follow me.” And Matthew rose and followed him.

Then, as Jesus sat at table in the house, a crowd of tax collectors and sinners came and joined him and his disciples for the meal. When the Pharisees saw it, they asked his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?” Jesus heard them and said, “People who are well do not need a doctor; sick people do. Go and learn what this saying means: ‘I want mercy, not sacrifice.’ For I did not come to call righteous people, but sinners.”

A question about fasting

Next John’s disciples came and asked him, “We fast often, and so do the Pharisees. Why do your disciples not fast?” Jesus answered, “How can the wedding guests mourn while the bridegroom is with them? But a time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them, and then they will fast. No one sews a patch of new, unshrunk cloth onto an old coat. The patch will pull away from the coat, and the tear will be worse. And people do not pour new wine into old wineskins. If they do, the skins will split, the wine will run out, and the skins will be ruined. No, they pour new wine into new wineskins, and both are kept safe.”

A leader’s daughter and a woman’s faith

While Jesus was still speaking, a leader came and knelt in front of him. “My daughter has just died,” he said. “But come and put your hand on her, and she will live.” Jesus got up and went with him, and so did his disciples.

Then a woman came up behind him. For twelve years she had suffered from bleeding. She touched the tassel on his cloak. She thought, “If I can just touch his cloak, I will be made well.” Jesus turned around, and when he saw her, he said, “Courage, my daughter! Your faith has made you well.” And from that moment the woman was well. When Jesus came to the leader’s house, he saw the flute players and the noisy crowd. “Go away,” he said. “The girl is not dead; she is asleep.” But they laughed at him. After the crowd had been sent outside, he went in and took the girl by the hand, and she got up. News of this spread through the whole region.

Two blind men

Two blind men followed Jesus as he left that place. They kept shouting, “Son of David, have mercy on us!” When he had gone indoors, the blind men came to him, and Jesus asked them, “Do you believe that I can do this?” “Yes, Lord,” they said. Then he touched their eyes and said, “Because of your faith, let it be done for you.” And their sight was restored. Jesus warned them sternly, “Make sure that no one hears about this.” But they went out and spread the word about him all over that region.

A man who could not speak

As they were leaving, some people brought to him a man who could not speak because he was controlled by a demon. When the demon was driven out, the man who had been mute began to speak. The crowds were astonished. “Israel has never seen anything like this!” they said. But the Pharisees kept saying, “It is by the prince of demons that he drives out demons.”

The harvest is large

Jesus went through all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, announcing the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every illness.

When he saw the crowds, he felt deep pity for them, because they were worn out and abandoned, like sheep with no shepherd. Then he said to his disciples, “The harvest is large, but there are few workers. So pray to the Lord of the harvest, and ask him to send out workers into his harvest.”
fields.summary: Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man, calls Matthew from the tax office and answers a question about fasting. A leader’s daughter is raised, a woman is healed by touching Jesus’s cloak, two blind men see and a man who could not speak talks; the harvest is large, but the workers are few.

fields.title: Matthew 10
fields.body_html:
Jesus names twelve apostles

Jesus called his twelve disciples to him and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to drive them out, and to heal every disease and every illness. The twelve apostles were these. First came Simon, known as Peter, with his brother Andrew; then James son of Zebedee, with his brother John; Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas, and Matthew the tax collector; James son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus; Simon the Cananaean, and Judas Iscariot, the man who betrayed him.

The twelve sent to the lost sheep of Israel

Jesus sent these twelve out, and he charged them: “Stay off the roads that lead to the Gentiles, and do not go into any Samaritan town. Go instead to the lost sheep, the people of Israel. Wherever you go, preach this: ‘The kingdom of heaven has come near.’ Heal those who are sick, raise the dead, make lepers clean, drive out demons. You received without paying, so give without charging. Do not provide yourselves with money for your belts, whether gold, silver, or copper. Take no bag for the road, no second tunic, no sandals, and no staff. Workers have earned their food. When you go into a town or village, ask who in it is worthy, and stay with that person until you move on. As you go into the home, greet the family. If that household is worthy, let your peace come to rest on it. But if it is unworthy, let the peace you gave come back to you. Some will not receive you or listen to your message. When you leave that house or that town, shake the dust from your feet. Truly I tell you, on the day of judgment the land of Sodom and Gomorrah will fare better than that town.

Sheep among wolves

Remember, I am the one sending you out, like sheep with wolves all around. So be shrewd like snakes, yet harmless like doves. Be on guard against people. They will hand you over to local councils and whip you in their synagogues. Because of me they will take you to stand before governors and kings. There you will bear witness to them and to the Gentiles. But when you are handed over, do not be anxious over how to answer or what to say. In that hour you will be given the words to speak. The speaker will not be you; it will be your Father’s Spirit speaking in you. One brother will hand another over to be killed, and a father his own child. Children will turn on their parents and send them to their death. Everyone will hate you because of my name. But whoever holds out to the end will be saved. If they hunt you down in one town, escape to the next. Truly I tell you, the Son of Man will come before you have completed your work in the towns of Israel.

No disciple ranks above the teacher, and no servant above the master. It is enough for disciples to become like their teacher, and for servants to become like their master. If they have called the head of the house Beelzebul, how much more will they insult the members of his household!

Fear God, not people

So do not be afraid of them. Everything now covered will be uncovered, and every secret will come to light. The things I tell you in the dark, you must say in the open; the things you hear as a whisper, you must proclaim from the housetops. Those who kill the body have no power to kill the soul, so do not be afraid of them. Be afraid instead of him who can destroy soul and body alike in hell. Two sparrows sell for a penny, do they not? Yet not one of them falls to the ground apart from your Father. As for you, even the hairs on your head have all been counted. So do not be afraid. You are worth more than a whole flock of sparrows.

So everyone who openly confesses me before others, I also will confess before my Father in heaven. But whoever denies me in front of people will be denied by me in the presence of my Father in heaven.

A sword that divides households

Do not imagine that my coming was to bring peace on earth. I came to bring a sword, not peace. My coming will set son against father, daughter against mother, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law. People’s enemies will be those of their own household. Whoever puts love for father or mother above me is not worthy of me, and whoever puts love for son or daughter above me is not worthy of me. Whoever refuses to pick up their own cross and walk behind me is not worthy of me. Those who secure their own life will lose it, and those who lose their life for my sake will find it.

Welcome and its reward

To welcome you is to welcome me, and to welcome me is to welcome him who sent me. Anyone who receives a prophet because that person is a prophet will be given a prophet’s reward; anyone who receives a righteous person because that person is righteous will be given the reward of the righteous. And whoever gives one of these little ones no more than a cup of cold water because that one is a disciple—truly I tell you, such a person will never lose their reward.”
fields.summary: Jesus names the twelve apostles and sends them to the lost sheep of Israel with authority to heal. Jesus warns that they go as sheep among wolves, tells them to fear God rather than people, and promises a reward to whoever welcomes them.

fields.title: Matthew 11
fields.body_html:
When Jesus had finished giving these instructions to his twelve disciples, he moved on from there to teach and to proclaim the message in their towns.

John’s question from prison

Meanwhile John, now in prison, heard about the works of the Christ. He sent word by his disciples and asked him, “Are you the one who is coming, or should we wait for someone else?” Jesus answered them, “Go back and tell John what you are hearing and seeing: the blind can see and the lame are walking, people with leprosy are made clean and the deaf can hear, the dead are raised to life, and the poor are hearing the good news. And blessed is the one who does not take offense at me.”

Jesus speaks about John

While they were on their way, Jesus started speaking to the crowds about John. “When you went out into the wilderness, what did you go to look at? A reed blowing back and forth in the wind? If not, what did you go out to see? Someone wearing soft, costly clothing? Those who dress in luxury are found in the palaces of kings. Why did you go out, then? To see a prophet? Yes indeed, I tell you, and he is even more than a prophet. This is the man of whom Scripture says, ‘I am sending my messenger ahead of you; he will make ready your way in front of you.’ Truly I tell you, of all who have ever been born of women, no one has appeared who is greater than John the Baptist. Yet even the smallest in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he is. From the time of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven has been suffering violence, and violent people are snatching at it. For all the prophets and the law spoke of what was coming, until John. And, if you will receive it, John is Elijah, whose coming was foretold. Whoever has ears must listen.

Children in the marketplace

What picture shall I use for the people of this generation? They are like children who sit in the town squares and call out to the other children, ‘We played the pipe for you, but you did not dance; we sang a funeral song, but you did not beat your breasts in grief.’ For when John came, he did not eat or drink as others do, and people say, ‘There is a demon in him.’ The Son of Man came and ate and drank, and they say, ‘Look at him! He eats too much and drinks too much, and he is a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet the deeds of wisdom show that she is in the right.”

Woe to the towns that did not repent

Then Jesus began to reproach the towns that had seen most of his mighty works, for they had not repented. “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! Had Tyre and Sidon seen the mighty works done among you, they would have turned from their sins long ago, dressed in sackcloth and sitting in ashes. But I tell you this: on the day of judgment Tyre and Sidon will be better off than you. And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted as high as heaven? No, you will go down to the realm of the dead. If Sodom had seen the mighty works done in you, it would still be standing today. But I tell you this: on the day of judgment the land of Sodom will be better off than you.”

Hidden from the wise, shown to little children

At that time Jesus said, “Father, Lord of heaven and earth, I give you praise, because you have kept these things hidden from the wise and the knowledgeable and have made them known to little children. Yes, Father, it pleased you to have it so.

My Father has entrusted everything to me. No one fully knows the Son except the Father, and no one fully knows the Father except the Son and those to whom the Son decides to make him known.

Come to me and find rest

Come to me, all of you who are worn out with work and weighed down with burdens, and I will give you rest. Put my yoke on your necks and learn from me, because I am gentle and my heart is humble. Then you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy to wear, and the load I give is light.”
fields.summary: From prison John the Baptist asks whether Jesus is the one who is to come, and Jesus answers and then speaks about John. Jesus reproaches the towns that did not repent and invites all who are weary to come and find rest.

fields.title: Matthew 12
fields.body_html:
Lord of the Sabbath

About that time Jesus was walking through the fields of grain on a Sabbath day. His disciples were hungry, so they started picking some heads of grain and eating them. The Pharisees saw it and said to him, “See there! Your disciples are doing something that the law forbids on the Sabbath.” Jesus answered them, “Do you not remember reading what David did when he and the men with him were hungry? He went into the house of God, and they ate the sacred bread set out before God. Neither David nor his men were allowed to eat it; only the priests were. Or have you not read in the law that every Sabbath the priests working in the temple break the Sabbath, and still they bear no guilt? I tell you, here is something greater than the temple. If you had understood what the words mean, ‘I want mercy, not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned people who have done nothing wrong. For the Son of Man is Lord over the Sabbath.”

Doing good on the Sabbath

Jesus left that place and went into their synagogue. A man was there whose hand was shriveled. They put a question to him: “Is healing allowed on the Sabbath?” They wanted a reason to bring a charge against him. He answered them, “Suppose one of you has just one sheep, and it falls into a hole on the Sabbath. Will you not grab hold of it and pull it out? And a human being is worth far more than a sheep! So the law allows doing good on the Sabbath.” Then he told the man, “Hold out your hand.” The man held it out, and it was made well again, just like his other hand. The Pharisees left and met together to plot against him, looking for a way to put him to death.

God’s chosen servant

Jesus knew what they were planning, and he withdrew from there. Many people followed him, and he healed every one of them. But he ordered them not to tell others who he was. This was so that the word spoken through the prophet Isaiah would be fulfilled: “See my servant, the one I have chosen, my dearly loved one, in whom my soul delights. I will place my Spirit on him, and he will make justice known to the Gentiles. He will not quarrel or shout; no one will hear him raising his voice in the streets. He will not snap off a bent reed or snuff out a wick that is barely burning, until he has led justice on to victory. And the Gentiles will put their hope in his name.”

By the Spirit of God

Then a man under the power of a demon was brought to him. The man was blind and unable to speak. Jesus healed him, and now the man could speak and see. The crowds were all beside themselves. “Might this man be the Son of David?” they asked. But the Pharisees heard it and said, “This man drives out demons only with the help of Beelzebul, the prince of demons.” Jesus knew what they were thinking, and he said to them, “Any kingdom that is split into warring parts falls into ruin, and any town or family that fights against itself will not last. So if Satan is throwing Satan out, he has turned against himself. In that case, how could his kingdom survive? And if I drive out demons with Beelzebul’s help, then whose help do your own people use when they drive them out? So they will be the ones to judge you. But if I am driving out demons by the Spirit of God, then God’s kingdom has already arrived among you. Or how could anyone break into the house of a strong man and make off with his goods, without tying the strong man up first? Only then can he strip the house bare. Anyone who does not stand with me stands against me. Anyone who does not help me gather is scattering. This is why I tell you that people can be forgiven every sin and every slander, but no one will be forgiven for blasphemy against the Spirit. A person who says something against the Son of Man may be forgiven. But a person who speaks against the Holy Spirit will find no forgiveness, not in the present age and not in the age that is coming.

Either count the tree good and its fruit good, or count the tree rotten and its fruit rotten. For the fruit shows what kind of tree it is. You family of snakes! How could good words come from you, since you are evil? The mouth speaks what spills over from the heart. From a good storehouse a good person draws out good things; from an evil storehouse an evil person draws out evil things. And I tell you this: every idle word people speak is a word they will have to answer for on judgment day. Your own words will declare you innocent, or your own words will condemn you.”

The sign of Jonah

At this some of the scribes and Pharisees spoke up. “Teacher,” they said, “we would like you to show us a sign.” He answered them, “An evil, unfaithful generation goes looking for a sign, but the only sign it will be given is the sign of Jonah the prophet. Jonah spent three days and three nights inside the great sea creature, and in the same way the Son of Man will spend three days and three nights deep in the earth. On judgment day the people of Nineveh will stand up alongside this generation and condemn it. They turned from their sins when Jonah preached. Yet here is something greater than Jonah. The queen from the south will stand up on judgment day alongside this generation and condemn it. She traveled from the far edges of the earth to listen to Solomon’s wisdom. Yet here is something greater than Solomon.

The unclean spirit returns

When an unclean spirit leaves a person, it wanders through dry country in search of a place to rest, but it finds none. So it says, ‘I will go back to the home I came out of.’ It returns and finds the place standing empty, swept, and set in order. Then it goes off and brings back seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they move in and settle there. In the end that person is worse off than at the start. And this evil generation will fare the same way.”

Those who do the Father’s will

Jesus was still talking to the crowds when his mother and brothers arrived. They stood outside, hoping for a word with him. Someone told him, “Look, your mother and brothers are standing out there. They are asking to speak with you.” Jesus answered the one who had told him, “Who is my mother? And who are my brothers?” He held out his hand toward his disciples. “Look,” he said, “these are my mother and my brothers. For anyone who does the will of my Father in heaven is a brother and sister and mother to me.”
fields.summary: Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath and heals a man on the Sabbath, fulfilling Isaiah’s words about God’s chosen servant. Accused of driving out demons by Beelzebul, Jesus answers that it is by the Spirit of God, offers only the sign of Jonah, and names as family those who do the Father’s will.

fields.title: Matthew 13
fields.body_html:
Parables by the lake: the sower

That same day Jesus left the house and sat down beside the lake. Such great crowds gathered around him that he got into a boat and sat down in it, while all the people stood on the shore. He told them many things in parables. “Listen!” he said. “A sower went out to sow. As he was sowing, some of the seed landed beside the path, and the birds came and ate it all up. Some landed on rocky patches where the soil was thin. They shot up at once, since the soil was not deep, but when the sun came up, the young plants were scorched, and having no root, they dried up. Other seed landed among thornbushes, and the thorns shot up and smothered it. But other seed landed in good soil and went on to bear grain, a hundred times as much as was sown, or sixty, or thirty. Whoever has ears must listen.”

Why Jesus speaks in parables

The disciples came up to Jesus and asked him, “Why are you using parables when you talk to them?” He answered them, “Because you have been allowed to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but they have not. Those who have will be given more, and they will have plenty. But those who do not have will lose even what they have. So I speak to them in parables, because they look without seeing and listen without hearing or understanding. In them the prophecy of Isaiah is coming true: ‘You will listen and listen and never understand; you will look and look and never perceive. This people’s heart has grown dull. Their ears barely hear, and they have shut their eyes tight. If they did not, they might see with their eyes and hear with their ears, understand with their heart and turn back, and then I would heal them.’ But your eyes are blessed, for they see, and so are your ears, for they hear. Truly I tell you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see the things you now see, and never saw them; they longed to hear the things you now hear, and never heard them.

The sower explained

As for you, then, hear what the parable of the sower means. Here is the seed sown beside the path: people who hear the message of the kingdom without understanding it. The evil one comes and carries off what was sown in their hearts. The seed sown on the rocky ground is the person who hears the word and at once accepts it with joy. But the word has no root in them, and they hold on only for a while. As soon as hardship or persecution comes on account of the word, they stumble and fall away. The seed sown among the thorns is the person who hears the word, but the cares of the present age and the false promises of wealth smother it, so that it yields no crop. But the seed sown on good soil is the person who hears the word and understands it. That person does bear fruit, yielding a hundred times what was sown, or sixty, or thirty.”

Weeds among the wheat

Then Jesus set another parable before them: “The kingdom of heaven is like the story of a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while people slept, an enemy of his came and scattered weeds all through the wheat, then went off. When the wheat came up and began to form heads of grain, the weeds showed up as well. The landowner’s servants came to him and said, ‘Master, surely it was good seed you sowed in your field? So where have these weeds come from?’ ‘An enemy has done this,’ he told them. ‘Shall we go out, then, and gather them up?’ the servants asked. ‘No,’ he replied, ‘for in gathering the weeds you might pull up the wheat with them. Leave them to grow side by side until the harvest. When harvest time comes, I will give the reapers their orders: “Pull out the weeds first, and tie them into bundles for burning. But store the wheat in my barn.”‘”

The mustard seed and the yeast

He gave them another parable to think about: “Picture a mustard seed that someone took and sowed in his field. The kingdom of heaven is like that. Of all the seeds it is the smallest, but once it is grown it stands taller than the other garden plants and turns into a tree, big enough for wild birds to come and nest among its branches.”

He told them another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like yeast. A woman took it and worked it into about 40 pounds of flour, until all the dough had risen.”

Everything Jesus said to the crowds he said in parables; indeed, he told them nothing at all without a parable. This was so that the word spoken through the prophet would be fulfilled: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will pour out what has been hidden since the world was founded.”

The weeds explained

Then Jesus sent the crowds away and went into the house. His disciples came to him and said, “Tell us plainly what the parable of the weeds in the field means.” He answered, “The sower of the good seed is the Son of Man. The field is the world. The good seed stands for the people who belong to the kingdom, and the weeds for the people who belong to the evil one. The enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels. The weeds are collected and burned up in the fire, and the end of the age will be like that. The Son of Man will send his angels, who will collect from his kingdom everything that leads people into sin and everyone who breaks God’s law. They will throw them into the burning furnace, and there people will weep and grind their teeth.

In their Father’s kingdom, then, the righteous will blaze out like the sun. Whoever has ears must listen.

Treasure, a pearl and a net

The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure buried in a field. A man came across it and covered it up again. Then, full of joy, he went and sold everything he owned and bought that field.

Or again, the kingdom of heaven is like a trader who was searching for fine pearls. When he came upon a single pearl of very high price, he went and sold off all his possessions and bought it.

Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet that was let down into the lake and pulled in fish of every kind. When it was full, they hauled it onto the beach, sat down, and sorted the good fish into baskets, while the worthless ones they threw away. The end of the age will be like this. The angels will go out and remove the wicked from among the righteous, and they will throw them into the burning furnace. There people will weep and grind their teeth.

Have you understood all this?” “Yes,” they answered. He told them, “That is why every scribe who has been trained as a disciple for the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who draws from his store of treasures both new things and old.” When Jesus had finished telling these parables, he moved on from there. Jesus came to his hometown and began teaching the people in their synagogue. They were astounded. “Where did this man get such wisdom,” they asked, “and these mighty works? This is the carpenter’s son, is it not? Is his mother not the woman called Mary? And are his brothers not James, Joseph, Simon and Judas? And are all his sisters not living here among us? So where did he get all this?” And they were offended by him. But Jesus told them, “Prophets are honored everywhere except in their own hometown and among their own family.” Because they would not believe, he did not do many mighty works there.
fields.summary: By the lake Jesus tells parables of the kingdom: the sower, the weeds among the wheat, the mustard seed, the yeast, the hidden treasure, the pearl and the net. Jesus explains them to the disciples, but in Nazareth the people take offense.

fields.title: Matthew 14
fields.body_html:
Herod and the death of John

Around that time, reports about Jesus reached Herod the tetrarch. “This is John the Baptist,” he told his courtiers. “He has been raised from the dead, and that is why he can do these mighty works.”

Herod had earlier arrested John, put him in chains and locked him in prison. He did it for the sake of Herodias, who had been the wife of his brother Philip. John had told Herod again and again, “The law does not allow you to have her.” He would have liked to put John to death, but he was afraid of the crowds, who looked on John as a prophet. When Herod’s birthday was being celebrated, Herodias’s daughter danced in front of everyone. Herod was so delighted with her that he swore to give her anything she asked for. Her mother told her what to say, and she answered, “Give me the head of John the Baptist on a platter, right here.” This grieved the king. Yet because of his oaths, and because of the guests at his table, he gave orders for her request to be granted. He sent word to the prison, and there John was beheaded. Someone carried the head in on a platter and gave it to the girl, and she in turn brought it to her mother. Then John’s disciples came for his body and buried it, and they went to tell Jesus what had happened.

Five loaves for a great crowd
